title: AEO analysis tools reviewed: What actually works in 2026
content:
The way people search for information is changing. Instead of scrolling through a list of blue links, more users are turning to AI-powered tools like ChatGPT, Google’s AI Overviews, and Perplexity that deliver direct answers to questions.
This shift has given rise to answer engine optimization (AEO), a discipline focused on optimizing content so it gets selected and surfaced by AI-driven answer engines rather than just ranked in traditional search results. AEO analysis helps teams understand where a brand currently stands in those answers and what to do about it.
This guide covers what AEO is, how it works, why it matters, and how to implement an AEO strategy.
AEO analysis measures how a brand is represented inside AI-generated answers. That includes whether the brand is mentioned by name, cited as a source, characterized favorably, or left out entirely for relevant prompts.
Traditional SEO analysis is built around the search engine results page — where a domain ranks for a given keyword, how many clicks and impressions it earns, and how that position shifts over time. AEO analysis works differently because answer engines do not return a ranked list of links. They return synthesized answers built from a handful of sources. That means there is no ranking position to track, only presence, framing, and share of voice.
An answer engine is a platform like ChatGPT, Gemini, or Perplexity that responds to a query with a direct, synthesized answer. Traditional search engines return a list of links and leave the user to decide which source to trust. An answer engine reads across multiple sources, pulls out the relevant information, and presents a single response, often citing the sources it drew from along the way.
The distinction matters for brands because answer engines are increasingly where buyers start their research. A brand that appears prominently and favorably in those answers has an advantage that does not show up in traditional SEO metrics. A brand that is absent or mischaracterized has a visibility problem that keyword rankings alone cannot diagnose.
Google Answer Box Optimization still matters. Structuring content to win the featured snippet at the top of a traditional Google search results page remains best practice. Featured snippets appear less frequently than they once did, but the structural habits that helped win them — clear definitions, concise steps, and well-formatted lists — are the same habits that support a strong AEO strategy .
Before comparing AEO analysis tools (not to be mistaken with SEO analysis tools ), it helps to establish what marketers should track.
Brand visibility is an AEO metric that counts how often AI platforms mention or cite a brand for specified prompts. It is a foundational metric in AEO analysis, though it has drawn criticism as a vanity metric since visibility does not always translate directly to clicks or conversions.
My perspective is that brand visibility is the prerequisite for clicks and conversions, not a substitute for them. Without visibility, a brand cannot get the click — and without the click, there is no conversion. That makes it essential to track, even if it sits earlier in the funnel than most marketers are used to measuring.
Research shows the value of visibility even when websites are not getting clicked. Responsive’s report, Inside the Buyer’s Mind , found that nearly as many potential buyers start searching with generative AI chatbots (32%) as with traditional web search (33%). In the Technology and Software industry, that number climbs significantly — buyers use generative AI for as many as 56% of searches.
HubSpot’s research shows a similar pattern of audience-specific AI adoption. According to HubSpot’s 2025 AI Trends for Marketers report, nearly 31% of Gen Zers default to chatbots or AI to find information online. Both findings point to the same conclusion: different audiences engage with generative AI at very different rates, which means brand visibility in AI answers matters more for some markets than others.
Pro tip: Knowing who’s in the audience and how they search helps determine how heavily to prioritize AEO analysis, though every brand stands to benefit from it.
This audience-level split shows up in HunSpot’s research on the CRM buying journey too.
HubSpot’s Q1 2026 Competitive NPS Survey of 3,063 CRM decision-makers found that 42% of CRM prospects use AI search as part of their evaluation, and AI search is the number one predictor of purchase intent across all six segments studied. AI search users are also deeper evaluators, completing an average of 4.1 evaluation activities versus 3.3 for non-users, and they lean more on analyst reports and ROI calculators rather than websites and third-party review sites.
The takeaway? Visibility in AI search earns brands a spot on the shortlist.
Once buyers form that shortlist through AI search, they typically follow up with a branded search to confirm and validate their choice before converting. By the time ‌branded search happens, the buyer has already done most of their evaluation.
Failure to earn brand visibility in AI is effectively a failure to make the shortlist of potential vendors. That makes visibility worth tracking closely. The challenge is that tracking it is harder than it sounds.
When someone asks an answer engine a question relevant to a brand’s category, marketers need to know whether the brand shows up. This sounds simple, but it quickly becomes complicated when there are multiple versions of the same prompt, user personalization, and multiple platforms. A brand might appear by name in one answer engine and be completely absent in another, even for the exact same prompt, because each engine pulls from a different mix of sources and weighs them differently.
Marketers can certainly get a feel for how a brand performs, but AEO analysis tools provide continuous monitoring so marketers can monitor progress.
For teams that want a fast read on where things stand today, HubSpot’s AI Search Grader is an excellent starting point.
AI Search Grader is a free tool that scores how ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity characterize a brand across five dimensions: sentiment, presence quality, brand recognition, share of voice, and market position. It gives marketers a baseline visibility snapshot before committing to a broader AEO (also called GEO ) strategy.
Because it’s free to run, marketing teams can use it on their own domain and on many competitors, which makes it a reasonable first move before investing time into a more detailed analysis.
The following screenshot shows how AI Search Grader summarizes performance for HubSpot:
The screenshot shows market position, which HubSpot dominates compared to competitors, and also mentions comparison mentions and common comparisons across the three core AI platforms: OpenAI, Perplexity and Gemini.
Citation analysis reveals which domains, content types, and source types influence AI-generated answers. A mention is any point where an answer engine references a brand by name inside a response. A citation goes further — the answer engine points to a specific piece of content as the source backing up a claim, and searchers can click through to visit the brand’s website.
The images below show the difference. A mention includes the brand’s name in the response without a clickable link. The screenshot shows HubSpot mentioned alongside four competitors in a table.
A citation is a clickable link within the answer, usually citing the website.
Both mentions and citations matter, but citations should probably carry a little more weight in the AEO analysis, because they signal that an answer engine trusts a brand’s content enough to treat it as evidence rather than just a name to drop. They are also the types of visibility that may lead to a click.
Pro tip: Marketers can actually track the impact of citations by reviewing referral traffic from AI platforms in GA4. This makes citations a really helpful KPI. Marketers can establish how many citations a brand is getting versus how many clicks resulted from a citation.
In my AI and SEO reporting , I include referral traffic from AI sources to help stakeholders see the benefit of AI. Brand visibility is great, but what really engages stakeholders us how that visibility translates to visits, conversions, and revenue. I also review conversions and conversion quality as part of my AEO analysis and take this information to stakeholders.
How a brand performs is one thing, but in isolation, marketers can miss the bigger picture.
This is where competitor share of voice comes in. Competitor share of voice measures how often a brand appears in an answer relative to the competitors who also show up for the same prompt. A brand might have solid visibility in isolation but still be losing ground if competitors are cited more frequently, more prominently, or in more favorable framing within the same set of answers. Tracking share of voice turns visibility from a standalone number into a competitive one, which is usually the more actionable read for a marketing team trying to prioritize where to invest.
Mention and citation counts are useful but mean more in context. Comparing a brand’s performance against industry benchmarks and tracking changes over time helps distinguish a brand-specific problem from a market-wide shift affecting the whole category.
Pro tip: HubSpot’s AI Search Sensor is a free dashboard that tracks AI answer engine volatility across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity — helping teams tell market-wide visibility shifts apart from gaps in their own AEO strategy.
The following image shows citation scores across the computer software industry. With this information, marketers can justify movements in AEO citations. For example, the computer software industry had an overall decline in early July. A drop during this time was industry wide and not site-specific.
One of the hardest parts of AEO analysis is the sheer range of ways people actually search with AI. Unlike traditional keyword search, where a handful of head terms capture most of the volume, prompts to answer engines are personalized, conversational, and long-tail — two people asking about the same thing do not write their prompt in the same way. That makes it practically impossible for marketers to track every individual prompt a brand might be surfaced or missed in, and trying to do so usually produces a pile of disconnected data points rather than a usable signal.
The issue is that AEO analysis means little if the prompts generated are inconsistent, which is what happens when marketers try and track too much manually. The more realistic goal is to track trends across prompt groups rather than chase individual prompts.
Prompt quality refers to how well a set of test prompts represents the broader categories an audience is likely to search. That includes branded queries, category questions, and competitor comparisons, grouped in a way that reflects real search behavior rather than an exhaustive list. A narrow or poorly grouped prompt set will produce results that look precise but do not represent how the brand is actually being discovered.
Testing repeatability is the other challenge. Answer engines are not static — the same prompt run twice in the same week can return different results depending on model updates, source availability, or minor phrasing changes. That variability makes it important to run the same prompt groups on a consistent schedule using consistent phrasing, so that changes in results can be attributed to genuine shifts in visibility rather than noise. Without repeatability, AEO analysis becomes a series of disconnected snapshots instead of a trend teams can act on.
This is where tooling earns its keep. Running prompt groups manually across three answer engines is not realistic to sustain by hand for more than a handful of prompts. HubSpot AEO tracks brand visibility across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini, handling the repeat testing and surfacing the pattern so marketers are not eyeballing differences manually.
The following screenshot shows prompt tracking with HubSpot AEO:
The console on the right shows how competitor visibility has changed compared to the brand.
A one-off AEO audit can tell a marketing team where they stand today, but it can’t tell them whether they’re improving. Building a repeatable framework turns AEO analysis from a snapshot into a process a team can actually run ongoing.
The starting point for any AEO analysis is a prompt set that actually reflects how a brand’s audience searches.
Category-level prompts are questions and comparisons someone would naturally ask when researching a solution in a brand’s space, not just questions that mention the brand by name.
Grouping these prompts by category or use case, rather than treating each one individually, is what makes the analysis manageable and repeatable. Instead of tracking dozens of individual prompt variations, a team can track a handful of prompt groups — say, “pricing questions,” “how-to questions,” and “comparison questions” — and watch how visibility shifts within each group. Grouping prompts turns the data into something usable: a dip or improvement in one group points to a specific type of buyer question a brand is winning or losing, rather than a vague, undifferentiated change in visibility overall.
Discovering prompts goes beyond pulling information from one source. Marketers should aim to build a big-picture view of the audience and how they search. Google Search Console is a useful place to build that list, since it already shows the queries a brand ranks for and the questions people are typing into traditional search. Those queries won’t map one-to-one onto AI prompts, but they reveal the underlying intent and phrasing patterns worth testing in answer engines as well.
A brand’s own customer-facing teams are an overlooked source for how audiences search. Support tickets, sales calls, and onboarding conversations are full of the language customers use to describe their problems — often before that language ever shows up in a search query. That phrasing is usually the closest thing to how a real buyer would phrase a question to an AI chatbot.
Combining category prompts, search console data, and customer-team insight produces a prompt set grounded in how people actually search, not how a marketing team assumes they search.
A prompt set is only useful if the results are captured consistently. For every prompt run, the goal is to document more than just whether a brand appeared — it’s to capture the full shape of the answer: whether the brand was mentioned by name, whether it was cited as a source, how it was framed (favorably, neutrally, or critically), which competitors appeared alongside it, and which sources the answer engine drew from to construct its response.
This level-of-detail matters because a “yes, we appeared” result on its own doesn’t say much. A brand mentioned once, buried below three competitors and described in neutral terms, is a very different result than a brand cited directly as the source behind the answer. Capturing evidence at this level of granularity — mention, citation, framing, competitor presence, and source — is what allows a team to actually diagnose why a result looks the way it does, rather than just knowing that it does.
This is where tools come in because it’s impossible to manage sentiment across every prompt.
HubSpot’s AI Search Grader shortcuts the manual work and delivers a benchmark fast, and for free. Rather than running prompts one by one and logging each result by hand, it scores a brand’s domain across five dimensions: sentiment, presence quality, brand recognition, share of voice, and market position. That gives teams a structured baseline read before building out a fuller evidence set.
AI Search Grader, shows the sentiment analysis with a single score, then quantitative information about the score.
Generally, marketers will re-run tests in accordance with the reporting schedule. This is often monthly, but some prompts might need more frequent analysis, like if new content is published or search marketers are trying to grow visibility within a particular category.
Frequent monitoring is fine, and it mirrors how most marketing teams already track Google Search Console clicks and impressions — checking in regularly is good practice, and letting an AEO tracking tool handle the actual re-running of tests removes the burden of doing it manually.
Where teams get into trouble is by reacting too fast to a single bad reading.
A drop in visibility for one prompt group in one week isn’t necessarily a sign that something’s gone wrong — it could just as easily reflect a model update, a shift in the sources an answer engine is favoring that week, or plain noise. Before reacting, it’s worth checking whether the dip is isolated to the brand or showing up industry-wide, and giving it a little time to settle before treating it as a genuine trend.
Monthly tracking is the sweet spot for actually understanding how visibility in AI search engines behaves over time — it’s frequent enough to catch real shifts, but far enough removed from day-to-day noise to reveal patterns, including seasonality and year-over-year changes that a single weekly check would never surface. This is exactly the context HubSpot’s AI Search Sensor is built to provide, helping teams tell whether a dip is a brand-specific problem worth investigating or an industry-wide shift that doesn’t need a reaction at all.
Here’s a screenshot from AI Search Sensor showing traffic trends from three platforms, ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity. Marketers can use it to establish benchmarks in referred traffic.
The AEO analysis tools below are split into two categories: those built for structured prompt audits and baseline scoring, and those built for ongoing citation and mention tracking.
The table covers core information about every tool, including engine coverage, depth of citation and mention analysis, competitor tracking, and whether the tool translates findings into specific recommendations rather than just reporting numbers. More information about each tool is found below.
HubSpot’s AI Search Grader is a free tool that gives marketers a structured, scored snapshot of how a brand is being represented across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. Marketers enter a domain — their own or a competitor’s — and the tool runs it through a fixed evaluation across five dimensions: sentiment, presence quality, brand recognition, share of voice, and market position.
Each dimension reports on a different piece of the visibility picture:
Because it is free and requires only a domain to generate a report, the grader has a few practical uses. Running it against a brand and its main competitors gives an instant read on share of voice gaps before deciding where to focus content efforts. A low presence-quality score despite decent brand recognition signals that the brand is known but not described accurately enough for an answer engine to draw from confidently. A weak sentiment score can reveal that AI is characterizing the brand in a way that does not match its actual positioning — often a sign that a competitor’s content is shaping the category narrative instead.
Because these are baseline, point-in-time scores rather than continuous tracking, the AI Search Grader is best used as a starting diagnostic — the tool that tells a team where to focus before they commit to an ongoing AEO analysis process.
Peec AI is a standalone AEO specialist, built entirely around AI visibility tracking rather than folding it into a broader SEO suite. It can track up to 11 AI platforms, including ChatGPT, AI Mode, AI Overviews, Microsoft Copilot, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-5 Search, DeepSeek, Qwen, and Mistral — though full platform coverage is reserved for Enterprise plans (see the pricing section below).
Pricing: Pricing with tools like Peec AI need serious consideration as on the surface they can look affordable, but costs scale fast as more platforms are added. For three platforms, it’s $80/month, but prices rise to $420/month to track six platforms. If you want to track all 11 AI platforms, then it’s custom pricing for Enterprise solutions.
What I like: It’s a clean, focused tool for a team that only needs tracking and doesn’t mind handling content creation elsewhere. It’s considerably cheaper than Profound and offers excellent platform coverage for the price.
HubSpot AEO is the product built for ongoing citation and mention tracking rather than a one-time diagnostic. It tracks key metrics for AEO success on a continuous basis, which means a team isn’t manually re-running prompts to check for changes — the tool is doing the repeat testing described earlier in this article’s framework section, and surfacing the results as a trend rather than a series of disconnected checks.
Where HubSpot AEO goes further than a scoring tool is in what it shows about why a brand appears — or doesn’t. HubSpot AEO shows which prompts cite your brand, which cite competitors, and where you are absent, breaking visibility down at the prompt-group level so a team can see exactly which category of question a brand is winning, losing, or missing from entirely. That level of detail is what turns a visibility number into something a content or growth team can actually act on, rather than a metric that just goes up or down without explanation.
Citation analysis shows what is actually driving answer engine behavior. Rather than guessing why a competitor is cited more often, teams can see whether answer engines are favoring comparison pages, third-party review sites, structured data, or a competitor’s own product documentation for a given prompt group. That pattern is nearly impossible to reconstruct manually across dozens of prompt runs and multiple answer engines.
HubSpot AEO also translates visibility findings into specific next steps. A gap driven by thin owned content surfaces as a content recommendation. A gap where competitors win through third-party mentions points toward outreach or PR. A gap tied to weak brand recognition suggests social amplification. That connection between finding and action separates HubSpot AEO from a pure monitoring dashboard.
Profound tracks up to nine AI engines — the broadest coverage of any tool in this roundup — but most of that coverage sits behind its custom Enterprise plan, which comes at a real cost. Marketers on the entry-level Starter tier only get ChatGPT, which may be enough for some brands, but it’s worth weighing where a target audience actually searches before assuming broader coverage is necessary.
Pricing: Starter is $99/month, tracking ChatGPT only with 50 prompts. Growth is $399/month and adds Perplexity and Google AI Overviews, with 100 prompts. Enterprise is custom-quoted and unlocks full nine-engine coverage, API access, and multi-region tracking.
What I like: Profound’s engine coverage at the top tier is genuinely unmatched, and it’s a serious option for enterprise teams that need multi-engine, multi-region tracking and are prepared to pay for it. The catch is that most of what makes Profound worth the price sits behind the custom Enterprise plan, so the entry-level Starter tier feels more like a taste than the full product. For brands that need visibility beyond the core platforms, Profound is a strong choice — but if all a team needs is ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini, there are more affordable options built specifically for that.
Semrush is a long-standing SEO platform that’s expanded into AI visibility through a dedicated AI Visibility module, tracking how brands appear across AI-generated answers alongside its existing search data.
Pricing: Semrush One (SEO and AI search) starts at $165.17/month, rising to $455.67/month, billed annually.
What I like: I’ve used Semrush for years, and I firmly believe that a tool already fluent in search and search behavior is one of the strongest possible partners for AEO. Semrush has been part of my own toolkit for a long time, and its AI Visibility module benefits directly from that legacy — it’s not a bolted-on afterthought, it’s built by a platform that’s spent years understanding how people search.
An AEO analysis score on its own doesn’t mean much without context. The most useful way to read AEO scores is relative — relative to a brand’s own baseline over time, and relative to the competitors showing up in the same prompt groups.
A brand recognition score of 60 might be strong in a young or fragmented category and weak in a mature one where competitors are consistently scoring in the 80s, so the number only becomes meaningful once it’s compared against something.
Not all signals carry equal weight. Citation status matters more than raw mention count — being cited as a source is a stronger form of visibility than being name-checked. Sentiment is most significant when it trends consistently in one direction across multiple engines and prompt groups, not when it fluctuates within a normal range. Share of voice is most useful as a comparative signal over time: flat absolute visibility alongside rising share of voice means a brand is closing ground on competitors even when the headline number has not moved.
Running an AEO analysis is, relatively speaking, the easy part. The harder part is knowing what to actually do with the results. This is where a lot of teams get stuck because a dashboard full of visibility, citation, and sentiment data doesn’t inherently tell anyone what to build, fix, or pitch next.
Tools that go beyond reporting and into recommendations close that gap.
HubSpot AEO is built around this specifically. For example, if there’s a citation gap, it’s reported via the tool, but there’s an important action assigned, like the specific next step to improve it. A gap caused by thinly owned content points toward a content brief; a gap where competitors are winning through third-party citations points toward outreach or PR; a gap tied to weak category-level recognition points toward social amplification to build broader signal. That translation from finding to action turns AEO analysis from a reporting exercise into a workflow a team can actually run.
Answer engines rely heavily on understanding what a brand is before they’ll cite it confidently. That means consistent naming, clear “about” and product pages, and structured data (like schema markup) that spells out who a brand is, what it offers, and how it relates to its category — reducing the ambiguity an AI model has to resolve on its own before it trusts a brand enough to reference it.
Answer engines tend to pull from content that’s easy to lift a clear, self-contained answer from — think direct definitions, clearly labeled steps, comparison tables, and FAQ-style sections that answer one question at a time. Long, unstructured prose that requires piecing together an answer across several paragraphs is harder for an answer engine to cite cleanly, even if the information itself is accurate.
Answer engines don’t rely on a brand’s own site alone — they weigh third-party sources, comparison content, reviews, and industry coverage too. Strengthening source coverage means making sure a brand shows up accurately in the kinds of places answer engines already trust: review platforms, industry publications, and comparison content that a category’s buyers are likely to consult.
Answer engines favor sources that reflect up-to-date information, particularly for pricing, feature, and comparison-style prompts. Outdated content — old pricing, deprecated features, stale comparisons — is a common, fixable reason a brand gets skipped over in favor of a competitor with more recently updated material.
HubSpot AEO makes the most sense for marketing teams that need ongoing, standalone visibility tracking across major answer engines, paired with clear direction on what to do with the results. It’s built for teams running AEO as a continuous process rather than a one-time audit — tracking brand visibility, citations, competitor share of voice, and sentiment on a rolling basis, and translating those findings into content, outreach, and amplification actions without requiring a separate tool to figure out next steps.
It’s a particularly strong fit for teams that don’t yet have AEO folded into a broader CRM-driven marketing workflow, but want a dedicated, purpose-built system for measuring and acting on answer engine visibility specifically. For a marketing or content team focused primarily on the AEO layer itself, HubSpot AEO covers that job end to end.
For teams already running their marketing operations inside Marketing Hub, AEO in Marketing Hub offers a more connected version of the same capability. Because it sits inside the same system that holds a brand’s customer and prospect data, AEO in Marketing Hub uses CRM data to suggest relevant prompts, which means prompt sets can be informed by the actual questions, deals, and customer profiles already living in the CRM, rather than being built from scratch in a separate tool.
This makes AEO in Marketing Hub the stronger fit for teams that want answer engine visibility to plug directly into existing lifecycle and campaign workflows — where a content gap surfaced by AEO analysis can flow straight into the same system already managing that brand’s broader marketing execution, instead of requiring data to be exported and reconciled between two separate platforms.
Most teams start seeing measurable shifts in visibility or citation patterns within four to eight weeks of acting on findings, though this varies by category competitiveness and how quickly content changes get indexed. Because answer engines update their source weighting frequently, some smaller shifts can show up sooner, but it’s worth waiting for a few testing cycles before treating early movement as a confirmed trend.
Category prompts generally deserve priority, since that’s where most buyers start before they know a specific brand name, and where competitors are most likely to be winning visibility instead. Brand prompts are still worth tracking to catch sentiment or accuracy issues, but category-level visibility tends to have a bigger impact on discovery.
Marketers often won’t need a developer to implement AEO changes because most AEO improvements are content and structure changes, like restructuring pages, adding FAQ sections, or updating outdated information. Developer involvement typically only comes in for structured data or schema markup, and even that’s often a lighter lift than a full technical SEO project.
Monthly tends to be the sweet spot for spotting genuine trends without reacting to short-term noise, though frequent monitoring through a tracking tool is fine as long as single dips aren’t treated as verdicts. Checking against industry-wide shifts before reacting to a brand-specific dip helps avoid overcorrecting on noise.
ROI from AEO is measurable. Teams typically connect it through downstream signals like branded search growth, behavior onsite from referral traffic from AI platforms where trackable, and share-of-voice gains against competitors over time, rather than a single ROI metric. As answer engine attribution tooling matures, this is likely to get more precise, but for now it’s best treated as a leading indicator alongside other marketing metrics.
AEO analysis is a must-have for all companies in 2026 and beyond. People are more confident searching using AI platforms, and it feels like this mode of search is here to stay.
HubSpot AEO is a stand-out tool for businesses who want AEO reporting — and importantly — actions for specific content, outreach, and amplification next steps, and for teams already working inside Marketing Hub, AEO in Marketing Hub takes that a step further by grounding prompt sets in real CRM data.
